projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Karl Goff was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of WWII Veteran Karl George Goff. Mr. Goff served in the Army Air Corpse, 8th Air Force, 445th bomb group, 703rd bomb squadron. He served in the Europe theatre and he was a prisoner of war. Karl's highest rank was staff sergeant. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Goff's home in Burton, Ohio, on September 6, 2002. Karl was eighty at the time of this recording. All right, where were you living when America entered WWII?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: In Burton, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. And still in school or out of school?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Oh, no, I was out of school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard the news about the Japanese attacking Pearl Harbour?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, there was a bunch of us laying up in my sister's house in front of the fireplace when it come over about Pearl Harbour and right then we were all going over there and kill those Japs. We were all going over there, we were going to get this over with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you tempted to go out the next day and sign up?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: We were. But -- well, a friend of ours, he was in the service, had been on furlough at that time, too. Everybody was pretty well upset.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But obviously you didn't go in right then. Did you wait to be drafted then?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, yes. I supported my mother and my grandmother and I could have stayed out, but I talked to my mother, I said, I have got to go in there, I have got to fight. So, I was drafted, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: October, 1942.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You drafted into the Army?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, yeah, I went in the Army and went to Camp Perry, where they give you these aptitude tests and stuff. And then I ended up going to New Jersey to the boardwalk, took more. I went into the Air Corps, that's right, in New Jersey. And up there, they test you again for what you are qualified to do, I guess. Well, I was slated to go to airplane mechanics school. My father had owned a garage since 1915, and of course I knew quite a bit about mechanics. Well, they opened up Laurie Two out in Denver, Colorado, and it was a gunnery school, Army gunnery school. So, they shipped use all out there, mechanics, gunners, radio operators. They wanted to fill up that camp in a hurry. So we all went out to Denver, and all I ever had in Atlantic City was schooling of soldier, left face, right face, about face, and that was about it. Never carried a gun. And I went out to Denver, went through Army school out there, and I became an instructor out there. And it was the CO, Laurie Two is a General Burwell, and he was kind of a lush. He liked his sauce, and we had class A passes for -- we had class A passes. We had no bed check. All we had to do was be there in time to teach our class and run, no callisthenics. We had garrison rations. Well, Walter Winchel heard about it, he came up and he played it up pretty big and they investigated. And they pulled General Burwell out and they put in General Sam Sneed. He was one of the Pearl Harbour boys. He was a little short guy, and he really pulled everything back. We went from garrison rations to field rations. They had callisthenics, we had bed checks, we had marching formation. We set a sleuth, wear dog chains all the time. He just made it miserable for everybody. So, we sang, "Let's remember Pearl Harbour when we were marching." He put our order out, everybody caught singing that song would be court marshalled. So he did away with that. He just got so, excuse the French, chicken shit, that I volunteered to go to gunnery school. And I went to Lorado, Texas, about four of us, went to Lorado, Texas. Went through gunnery school. And from gunnery school, we went up to -- well, when I left Lorado, Texas, they were headed up for Nebraska, Lincoln, Nebraska and I was, had an awful headache and sore throat and just didn't feel good. I went in sick call and they give me some aspirin and nose drops, and I crawled in the bunk on this train. And they carried me off up in Lincoln, Nebraska, I had the meningitis. Well, then they sent my mother a telegram and she come out there. And I remember waking up and there was sitting my mother, you know. And that's, I got well enough to get out of the hospital. They sent me home for two weeks to recuperate and then back to Lincoln, Nebraska. Well, in the meantime, all these guys I enlisted with had all been signed to crews and were gone. So I was put on a make up list, I guess, and they formed us a crew up there and we went from Lincoln, Nebraska, after the crew was formed. Our pilot was Lieutenant Murray and our co-pilot was Lieutenant Rohall. Our bombardier was Lieutenant Cantos. Radio operator was Roy Williams and nose runner was Ted Kollaski, which then changed his name to Ted Kay. Our engineer was Joe Roberts, I was the right waist gunner. Vincent LaSconny was the left waist gunner, and Jimmy, the tail gunner. Houston. Jimmy Houston from Pennsylvania, was our tail gunner. And we all went to Davis Mountain Field in Tucson, Arizona. We took overseas training. And after that, we went to Kansas City, Kansas for the crew, and they didn't have enough planes, so they drew straws and we took, we had to go over by ship. And I think about five crews that got to fly their plane over, but we went over by ship. And landed in South Hampton and they took us up to, Norwich, somewhere in Norwich. They put us in a replacement center. Well, the 445th bomb group had just had a raid and they lost a lot of planes, so we were sent to the 445th bomb group, 703rd bomb squadron, which years ago, it wasn't, he wasn't there when I was there, but Jimmy Stewart was the commanding of the 703rd, and but when we got there, they transferred him up to wing, but we have the history of being in Jimmy Stewart's squadron. And from there, we started our mission. We flew, I flew 22 missions with my regular crew. Come the 23rd mission, the lead crew that was on pass from London, didn't get back, so they had to make up a lead crew. So they took the pilot and co-pilot from one crew, his name was, the pilot was Winters. I don't remember what the co-pilot was. And they took the bombardier and navigator from another crew, and they had a First Lieutenant flying the nose tour to make up a mission. They had the engineer and radio operator from another crew, and I was in the back with, they took our tail gunner and left waist gunner, me being the right waist gunner, made up the back, made up the crew. And we didn't make it back. We got hit going down a bomb run. I remember the nose gunner said, "Hey, that first burst was right outside here." Well, flack come up in the valley of four. Boom, boom, boom, boom. And the other three come into the ship. And it blew me back over the escape hatch. Luckily, I had my parachute hooked on one side of my harness, because I just opened up the escape hatch and tumbled out with the chute hooked on one side. Had the flack suit on, it busted off as soon as I hit the air stream, I guess. And my chute opened and I didn't have any problem. But I never thought to look whatever happened to the ship. And after we got down to the ground, there is a crew that crash landed after we did, and they said the ship was blown apart. So out of the ten, only four of us got out. Bombardier, navigator got out of the nose, the engineer got out, jumped out of the bomb bay, and I went out the escape hatch in the back. But, when we hit the ground, I couldn't spill my chute because it was only hooked on one side and I couldn't reach the shrouds. And just as I was going to hit, the darn wind hit the chute and set me up and I come right down on my neck, shoulder and my fleet flew over, flopped and hit me in the head and dragged me up across the field. And the German civilian stopped to shoot. Well, I stood up and this one little German, he, all I could figure out was his family was killed in a bombing raid and he had no use for the air corps, apparently. And I stood up and he come up and sputtered something in German and hauled off and hit me and knocked me down. But I bounced right back up. And I thought well, I'll show him, but damn, he hit me again and this time I stayed down. And they started kicking me so I just curled up in a ball as tight as I could. And they were kicking me and hollering German names at me. Then I heard some other louder German, and I looked up and here the Luffas was ready to pull guns on the civilian, they chased him back off of me. And I got up and they took me into Magdeburg. That's where we were shot down in Magdeburg, and put me in jail, searched me and everything else. Then put us in, while I was in jail, they brought in the bombardier, the navigator and the engineer. And I was kind of glad to see them because I thought maybe I got excited and bailed out and I shouldn't have, you know, I thought maybe -- because I didn't think to look for the plane. I guess there was nothing to see anyhow. But we kind of talked to see what happened, nobody seemed to really know exactly because it happened so fast. And then they took us to Frankfurt on the Rein and put us in solitary confinement. And every day that, you'd hear them clump, clump, clump, down the hall, all, one at a time, each to be interrogated. And we'd give them our name, rank and serial number. That's all we are supposed to. And then back to solid we go. Well, this went on for a couple three days, then finally, they come and got me and they brought me to this room. Well, there was our bombardier that was on that ship. I recognized him. And interrogator says, "Do you know this officer here," and I says, "No, I don't." He asked the officer, "Do you know this sergeant here," and he said, "Yeah, that's Sergeant Goff, he was the gunner on our crew." And so they released the officer and they told him he could go and I thought, oh boy, this is where I get it. But the interrogator was from Chicago. He was a German but he lived in Chicago, and when the war broke out, he went back to Germany as an interrogator. And he called me up and he says, "Here, I want to show you something, Sergeant Goff." He did a map of our air base, he knew more about the air base than I did. He knew the cook's name, and their phone numbers. And he offered me a cigarette. He says, well, he said, you can go. And he let me go. They put me on the compound. Well, this is pretty good. So, I found this lieutenant, and I didn't call him sir or anything else, but I said, you know, what are you trying to do, you know, you ratted in there. He was, oh, I couldn't stand it in that solitary cell no more, he said, I banged my head and I bailed out, they were just killing me. I was just going nuts in there. I go, thanks a lot. I said you could have got me in a lot of trouble. And that's the last I ever saw of him. So, then they put us on a sparks on troop train in these forty nat cars and we headed for Nuremberg. Well, we got striked once on the way because this train was shooting off sparks and the RAF, they didn't know who was in that train. But we were lucky none of our crew was, bunch got hit. So we went on to Nuremberg and Loofah, I can't remember, Loofah, I don't remember it, but we were there over Easter. I was shot down, by the way, on March 3, 1945. So I didn't have much time as a prisoner, but long enough. And at Easter Sunday, we were still at Nuremberg. Well, then we left Nuremberg and they marched us, we didn't know where we were going, they marched us. We ended up in Moosburg. But our second day out of the march, we got hit by our fighters. They thought we were a German column, I guess. And everybody ran and hid behind trees and stuff, even the guards did. And they wiped out quite a few guys. And I was at the tail end of the column, which didn't get hit and the front end didn't get hit. It was right in the middle that got it. Well, they got us all assembled again and we had to march by these guys moaning and groaning, help me, help me, and we couldn't do anything to help them. But the next day on the march, here comes a P-51 again. And we all start to go to scramble and major was head of the prisoner of war hollered, stand fast. So we did. And the plane just went alongside us and wobbled its wings, so we knew that their gun cameras had picked it up. So every day after that, there would be one of our planes following us along, keeping track of us. Well, we ended up in Moosburg, Stalach 7-A. And we were there, oh, the camp was just packed. There was four of us, we each had a blanket and we made a little tent in the corner of a fence and we stayed in that. Well, this one morning, we could hear this rumbling and we look -- well first we saw this Liason, small Liason airplane up there. We figured they are looking for targets for artillery. Pretty soon we hear the rumble, and here come some tanks up over the hill. And the German guards come down out of those towers and they hid amongst us and the SS were shooting them and then we were going up to man the towers ourselves. And you could see the tank muzzle gun go boom, no tower. It was Patton's 3rd Army that come up through and liberated us. And after we were liberated, they marched -- they drew straws on which compound was going to leave first. Well, we got, we were lucky, we got to go first. So we matched out into a large area of open fields where our allied airplanes come in, these VC-3's, to pick us up. Well, in front of us was a bunch of limies, and they didn't want to give us, let us go in front of them. They argued for a while and finally our planes took off, went back. The next day they come back and we got things straightened out. The limies got to the side and we got on our planes and they flew us back to Camp Lucky Strike in France. Mahara, France, where first thing they did was you throw all your clothes in a pile and you walk through the delousing and into the showers. And they give you some clean clothes on the other side. A little food because all we had to eat was, on the march, was once in a while we got a Red Cross parcel. But one time on the march, one soldier, I don't know how he did it, but he grabbed a chicken and it never made any noise. That night when we stopped, we killed the chicken and roasted it and our group had a little bit to eat. But at Camp Lucky Strike, they put us on kind of little diets. They said our little tummies were red and sore, you know, we had to watch what we ate. Which didn't seem to bother my stomach any. And then they laid us, put us on one of these Kaiser Liberty Ships, maiden voyage, brought supplies over and we got on it to head back to the United States. And just before we docked, they declared North Atlantic waters noncombatant. So we could sit up on the deck of the ship and smoke. And the next morning we went in, past the Statute of liberty and docked in Boston Harbour, and they loaded us on trains and took us to Camp Antebury, Indiana, where we got a set of new clothes. And they sent me home for -- well, it was going to be for 30 days. At the end of 30 days, I got a telegram, you got a 30 day extension, they weren't ready for us. At the end of that 30 days, we got another 30 day extension, made it 90 days altogether. I was home all that whole summer. And then they sent us down to Miami Beach, Florida, where they interrogated us and started up this number system to get discharged, and they flew us from Miami Beach to Texas to -- that big air base in Texas, Fillery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I can't think of which one.

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Anyhow, they flew us there, and started our discharge system. Well, I no sooner got started and I got sick, so I had to go to the hospital. And when I got out of the hospital, that put me clear back to the end of the line again. Well, in the meantime, they opened up a separation center at Greensboro, North Carolina. So they said any of those living east of the Mississippi River, could go to Greensboro, North Carolina to be discharged. So, we all did but they said just remember this, you are on your own. The longer it takes you to get to Greensboro, the longer it's going to be for your discharge because whenever you get there, you are going to be at the end of the line. Well, guys are getting off because they, when they got east of the Mississippi, they lived in these little towns, they would get off and drive there and get their car, they didn't care. But made no sense to me, I lived in Ohio, so I stuck it out. And we were one of the first few that went through the discharge at Camp, at Greensboro, North Carolina. They give me a little travel pay, put me on a bus and sent me home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in the camp in Moosburg before you were liberated?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, I think about four days. Because it was, everybody knew that, well Roosevelt died while we were marching. We heard that. But the German guards there when we were marching would take maybe four or five Americans and they said they'll get them back to the American lines and the Americans would take care of the German guards. Well, some of them got away, but then come back up the DSS is back there shooting them, so nobody went on from there, they slept with the group.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And how long was that march?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Oh, God, I don't know. When was Easter?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would be probably early April, I think, right?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: We were liberated --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Easter changes. Late March, early April I guess. So, where did that march start?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: It started in Nuremberg.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that an interrogation camp?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: No, it was just a Luffa camp. I can't think of the number of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you were there, what, maybe a month or so, a little more than that?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Probably about a month, I'd say, at Nuremberg.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like at the Nuremberg camp?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, they didn't have anything to eat. We would get a few Red Cross parcels, pooled them and we had a little kitchen, and then we would, maybe two would be together, and then we'd all go up in a group and eat. But there was, I don't know whether this had anything to do with it or not, but they used to bring, well, I guess sauerkraut and stuff in, they had a team of horses and a wagon and a barrel of it, I mean we had that. Then one day, only one horse was pulling the wagon and we had meat in with the sauerkraut, so we didn't know if it was horse meat or what, but we ate it. Then with the Red Cross, we got by. Lost some weight, but that didn't hurt anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have Luffas guards there at that camp?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the treatment okay?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, they treated, I had a few little wounds on, they took care of. They had a doctor there and they took care of me. But they, even the Germans didn't have anything to eat. We had this broke, you know, bread made out, it had sawdust in it, you know, you try and toast it and the it would glow like wood because -- but white lard and broke, that's about what the Germans were eating. And the German guards and the German people, well you can see why the people were upset, like that one guy that hit me, but the main rotten, those were the Natzi's, the SS. And we would be walking through a little town and those little buggers would come out and kick us and spit at us and throw things at us. Of course, now they are, I don't know how old they would be now. They would be sixty some years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, what did you do to pass the time in the Nuremberg camp? Did you have anything to keep you occupied?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, we played Penuchle. We had a deck of cards and we made up a Penuchle deck. And most of the time we would play cards and other times we would walk a lot. Just around the inside of the camp to keep from getting stiff, I guess. We had little tents to sleep in on boards. We were off the ground, but just boards we slept on. And as I say, we played cards and talked, talked about food.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, let's see you probably got to England some time in late 44, is that right, middle 44, when you arrived overseas in England?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, it was in the fall. We left here October 44, to go over to England.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like in England?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Oh, that was nice. They, the English, they appreciated us. We got a couple passes once, the R&R passes. As we flew so many missions, we went into London and they would get in a squabble with the English soldiers, you know. It was God save the queen and we had other words and that would always start a fight. But, other than that, I mean, we got along all right with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first mission?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any specific memories you could share about that?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: No, it was really nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were most of your missions into Germany?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, Germany and France. The mission was Starburken, railroad marching yard, flack was very light, no enemy fighters, fighter support was fair, bomb through the clouds, temperature was minus 34 degrees up there. Total of six hour and twenty-five minute flight.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that an average length for a mission for you?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: No, we have gone on a flight of nine hours.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were some of the roughest targets that you had to hit?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Magdeburg. That's where I got shot down. We were there a couple times to Magdeburg. But mostly our biggest trouble was flack because they were kind of, when they come out with the P-51 to fly escort, they had the range, they could follow us all the way to the target. But they did the P-47, they couldn't. And that's when they used to get it. And the P-47 would drop back and then the bombers were on their own. But when they went out with the P-51, they could follow us all the way. In Germany, we didn't have too many fighters either left. So, it was the tail end of the war, it was going downhill.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you don't remember any other rough missions before the mission you were shot down?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, they were all scary, but we got flack rattle in the plane before, but nothing like when we were shot down. We never heard anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your original crew make it, did they --

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: They finished up, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They finished up?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, they got in their 35 missions and they come back. Well, we tried, our nose gunner and I kept in contact, real close. In fact, when I got back to the States, I went up to New York to see him. And we would try to locate our other crew members, but Vince Sprawly and Jimmy Houston were killed, they didn't make it out. We found our co-pilot, we found our navigator, we found our bombardier, found our engineer, and nose gunner and myself. We used to, the pilot -- our navigator said he run across the pilot once up in Chicago, but he said he didn't look good so he figured he must have died. And the radio operator, Roy Williams, we never found out what happened to him. They have all the ways of looking up, you know, crew member stuff, by they never could come across him. They don't know what happened. So, the most ever got together was four of us at one time after the war, and that was out in California at a Second Air Division reunion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you close to the entire crew? Did you have one particularly close buddy?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: No. Probably Jimmy and Ted were probably the closest to us. We always hung around together anyhow.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do for fun in England with those guys?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, when we weren't flying, we went to Norwich, bummed around, went to the NCO club there on the base. We done a lot of flying. We did four days straight once. That kind of wears you out, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the longest mission you flew?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: I don't, I think it was about nine hours.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the target?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Munich is a pretty long run.

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Seven hours, eight hours and thirty-five minutes. Probably the longest one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Geberstat? I think that's it?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That must be in Germany, I assume?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, it would be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, you obviously had limited fighter opposition, but did you ever get to shoot off any rounds?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. The day we were shot down, we got hit with German jetties. The first ones we ever seen, so as we shot --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many were up there?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: German jets.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: One come out of the sun. They lined up on us. We were the lead crew that day and they went by so fast, I didn't see them coming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was he trying to accomplish anything or just showing off the jet?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: I don't know if they got anybody else, hit anything else, I don't know. Because the crew that went down behind us got hit by flack. They got the engines knocked out and they crash landed. This one said our plane was blown right in half. You couldn't prove it by me. I didn't hear no buzzer to bail out or anything, I just went.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the usual procedure, is that you would get some kind of a buzz from the --

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Pilot, yeah. But the flight deck must have been pretty well wiped out. But the radio operator, or the engineer got out of the flight deck. Of course he was cleared by the bomb bay. And the nose guy didn't get, but the bombardier and navigator got out, which were between the flight deck and the nose gear down underneath on a B-24. God only knows how. My time wasn't up, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you flew B-24's?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: B-24's you flew?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you like that plane?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, it was a good plane. It was, we had more range than a 17, we carried a bigger mountain load than the 17 and we had more speed than the 17. But they didn't glide worth a darn. Like a 17, you know, you lose the engines. And they had a Davis, called a Davis wing, short wing, had a lot of lift. The B-17 had a wide wing span, and they would glide, but B-24 didn't. If you lost all your engines, forget it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that because the B-17 could stay out there with one engine because it had --

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: It could stay up there with two, but I don't think they could stay up there with one. We got to fly with one or two. But if there were two out, you had to throw about everything you had in there out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember mail call, getting letters from home, either before or after you were captured?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, yeah, we got them before, we got mail from home. But as soon as we got to Stalach 78, Moosburg, some of the soldiers, they give us e-mail and I sat down and wrote e-mail to my mother right away. In fact, she got that before the government notified her that I was back in the Army's hands.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you were just able to write that and give it to the Red Cross and then they would deliver it?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: They must have delivered it to the post office up here and of course the lady over at the post office saw it. She opened it up and read it. Well, her son and I were good friends and he was in the Air Force, too. And of course then she went down to my mother right away. I got that in here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, before you were captured, what kind of things would you write about? Did you write about much?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: No, you could write a little bit about missions, but not too much. I don't know how much they did ever blank out. Mostly asked for how you are at home, and we are fine, don't worry about us, send a cake or some cookies.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did those arrive safely?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get the cake and cookies without it being crushed?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, sometimes the cookies were a little sad but they were eatable.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does any one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Just when we were shot down. I mean, it stays with you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Obviously that happened so fast, what was going through your mind?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, it happened fast.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't really have time to think about what was going on, right?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: No. The only other thing we had one time, to recall us from the original, we was going to go to Berlin and they changed it to Brunswick, and then they recalled the mission for some reason or other. And coming back, we couldn't get to our base because it was all fogged in. And that's one thing about England, God, you would sweat getting back more than anything because you couldn't get to your base half the time. And so we were flying the coast trying to find an open spot, getting about ready to bail out because we were running out of fuel. And they happened, our pilot happened to spot a break in the fog and stuff and he saw this little deserted air strip and so we went down and landed and it was a spitfire base, he put a B-24 down on a spitfire base. And we stayed there that night and they give us fuel and stuff. And the next morning, we took off and went back to our base. But, it always kind of irked me, the English charged our government for breakfasts and logging. And gas that we sold maybe ninety cents a gallon, they charged us two dollars something a gallon for the same gas we got on a lease. That kind of burns you up, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, how did you learn about that, or did you just know that was the way it worked?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Well, that's the rumor that goes around.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They sent the bill.

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: But that's --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you dating?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Yeah, I was engaged at that time, but then we got back and we broke up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you finally got back home?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Terrific. Yeah, we -- well, we got home in October. I know my mother had two roast chickens. I think I ate one of them myself. And my sisters and, my one brother-in-law wasn't back out of the service yet. My other brother was, he never went in the service, he was an undertaker in Littlefield. But we had some proud moments, I want to tell you. They half-expected to see me come up there all shot up or something, and we got off the terminal in Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life when you were back?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Not one bit. Of course I had ninety days at home before I was discharged. I don't know, that's about all I can tell you about it, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There was a question that just slipped my mind. I'm getting old. I can't remember. You think that covers it then?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Pretty much. There is some details --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you about. You said you heard about FDR when you were on that march?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did the German guards tell you about that?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: We heard it on the radio going by, in Southern Bulgaria we were marching, and it come over, FDR, and we picked up that he was dead.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction of the guys when they heard that?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: I don't think they really cared. I mean, it was probably tragic, but I know we were just so worn out that we didn't really care, I don't think. We knew that the war was about over and we was on the winning side.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Obviously, after what you had been through, you wouldn't have been sent to Japan, but what did you think when you heard about the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: I thought it was great. I'm glad that Truman did that. Saved a lot of lives. That would have been a tough one to conquer, Japan. And they deserved it, I think. They didn't hesitate Pearl Harbour.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, you certainly had enough points. They wouldn't have sent you over there, right?

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: I doubt it, although I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I can't believe they would send a former POW over there.

sp.speaker: Karl Goff
sp.p: Because I was still in the service. I mean, see I was still home on furlough when Japan surrendered. I was so glad of that.
